name: Diosmin (incl. micronized purified flavonoid fraction with hesperidin)
short: Case reports: DRESS, a severe drug reaction (one with very high liver enzymes), after diosmin-hesperidin. Phlebotonics, class-wide: slightly more adverse events. Raised carbamazepine levels (12 men).
text: A 2020 Cochrane review of placebo-controlled trials of oral phlebotonics for chronic venous insufficiency (covering rutosides, hidrosmine and diosmine, calcium dobesilate, Centella asiatica, aminaftone, French maritime pine bark extract and grape seed extract) pooled adverse events from 37 studies with 5789 participants and found that phlebotonics as a group probably increase adverse events slightly compared with placebo (risk ratio 1.14, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.27; moderate-certainty evidence), most often gastrointestinal disorders; the trials gave only short-term safety data, and the abstract gives no adverse-event figures for diosmin separately nor says which diosmin preparations were tested. For the micronized purified flavonoid fraction (90% micronised diosmin with 10% flavonoids expressed as hesperidin, taken by mouth), a 2003 review reported a tolerability profile similar to placebo in clinical trials, with mostly gastrointestinal and autonomic adverse events, and a meta-analysis of 22 randomised trials (2,335 participants) after haemorrhoid surgery reported no substantial effect on adverse reactions. Two case reports describe drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), a severe skin and systemic reaction for which one report gives a mortality rate of 3.8-10% (a figure for DRESS in general, not for diosmin), after diosmin with hesperidin; in one, a 34-year-old woman had markedly raised liver enzymes and, two months later, a relapse of the rash and raised liver enzymes with a positive herpes simplex IgM test, and she had also taken a systemic sunscreen product beforehand; the abstracts do not say whether the micronized fraction was used. In open-label studies in 12 healthy male volunteers each, 10 days of diosmin (the abstracts do not say whether it was micronized) raised blood levels of single doses of carbamazepine (attributed to CYP3A4 inhibition) and fexofenadine (attributed to P-glycoprotein inhibition); these were pharmacokinetic studies and the abstracts report no clinical outcomes.
